opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that AI can contribute at almost every stage of the pipeline, but the nature of the contribution changes a lot depending on where you are.

At the very front end, in basic research and target discovery, a lot of the bottleneck is just the sheer volume of knowledge. There are millions of papers, enormous genomics and proteomics datasets, clinical observations scattered across the literature. A scientist can only read so much. Models that can reason over that literature, connect findings across fields, and help generate hypotheses are genuinely useful there. It's less about replacing the scientist's judgment and more about widening what they can hold in their head at once.

Then in the lab itself, there's experimental design and analysis. Researchers spend a surprising amount of time on things like writing analysis code, troubleshooting protocols, figuring out why an assay isn't behaving. Having a capable assistant that can help plan experiments, interpret messy data, or suggest what to try next can compress iteration cycles quite a bit.

In the more chemistry- and biology-specific stages, like molecule design, protein engineering, and predicting properties such as binding, toxicity, or solubility, you have specialized models that have made real progress. And I think increasingly the interesting work is in combining those specialized tools with general reasoning models that can orchestrate them, almost like a research agent that knows when to call a structure predictor or a docking tool and how to interpret the results.

Further downstream you get into clinical development, which is where a lot of the time and cost actually lives. Trial design, patient recruitment, identifying the right endpoints, handling regulatory documentation. That's a lot of text, a lot of process, a lot of coordination. Language models are a natural fit for parts of that, and even modest efficiency gains there can matter a lot because the stakes and the timelines are so large.

I'd add one caveat, though. Biology is still fundamentally empirical. A model can suggest a beautiful hypothesis, but at some point you have to run the experiment and see if the cell or the patient agrees. So I see AI as something that makes the loop between idea and evidence faster and smarter, not something that lets you skip the evidence. If we get that right, the payoff could be fewer dead ends, faster paths to good candidates, and ultimately medicines reaching patients sooner.

r001.rationale: The response mentions regulatory documentation and downstream efficiency, but does not identify accelerating the FDA approval process as a role for AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that AI is contributing unevenly across the pipeline, and the places where it's furthest along aren't always the ones people talk about most.

Start at the very beginning, the hypothesis stage. There's an enormous amount of biology sitting in papers, patents, internal lab notebooks, and public datasets that no single person can hold in their head. Language models are genuinely good at reading all of that and helping a scientist ask, "What's the evidence that this target matters in this indication, and what's the counter-evidence?" That's not glamorous, but target selection is where most of the downstream failure gets baked in. If you pick the wrong biology, nothing you do later saves you.

Then there's the structural and molecular layer, which is where the big headline results have come from. Protein structure prediction changed what a computational chemist can do on a Tuesday afternoon. You can go from a sequence to a plausible structure to docking candidates in a way that used to take months. Generative models for small molecules and antibodies are now producing candidates that are actually synthesizable and testable, not just pretty pictures. The caveat I always give is that the model's output is a hypothesis, not an answer. The wet lab is still the source of truth.

Where I'm personally most excited is the loop between prediction and experiment. The real leverage isn't a model that's right 90 percent of the time. It's a system that proposes an experiment, a lab runs it, the result comes back, and the model updates. That closed-loop design, with automated labs and models that know what they're uncertain about, is what compresses the timeline. You're not replacing the scientist, you're letting them run twenty hypotheses in the time it used to take to run two.

Further down the pipeline, in preclinical and clinical work, the contribution looks different. It's less about discovery and more about reducing waste. Predicting toxicity earlier, finding the patient populations most likely to respond, designing trials that need fewer participants to get a clean signal, and pulling structure out of messy clinical notes. These don't make for exciting demos, but a failed Phase II trial costs more than a decade of early research, so even modest improvements there matter enormously.

I'd add two notes of caution. First, the data problem is real. Biology data is noisy, batch-dependent, and often collected under conditions the model never sees described. A lot of the work is boring data engineering, and teams that skip it get fooled. Second, the field has a tendency to overclaim. We don't yet have a drug that went from an AI-generated hypothesis all the way to approval with the model doing most of the work. We have a growing number in trials, and that's meaningful, but we should let the clinical results speak before we declare victory.

So the short version: AI is already a real accelerant in reading the literature, in structure and molecule design, and in cutting waste in development. The transformative part, the closed loop between models and automated experiments, is just starting, and that's where I'd be watching over the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response mentions improving trial design and reducing development waste, but it does not identify accelerating the FDA approval process as a potential role for AI.

astra-6.text:
I think AI can contribute across the entire pipeline, from understanding the biology of a disease to designing a molecule and figuring out whether it can safely help patients.

Early on, it can help researchers connect information across scientific literature and experimental data to identify promising targets. In drug discovery, it can help generate candidate molecules and prioritize which ones to test. Further downstream, it can support clinical trial design and help researchers understand why different patients respond differently to a treatment.

What’s especially exciting is the feedback loop between AI and experiments. A model proposes a hypothesis, scientists test it, and the results inform the next hypothesis. That could help us learn more from each experiment and explore ideas we might otherwise miss.

But biology is incredibly complex. A compelling prediction still needs experimental validation, and a promising molecule still needs rigorous clinical testing. The opportunity is to help scientists make better decisions throughout that process, so we can ultimately bring effective treatments to patients more efficiently.

r001.rationale: The response mentions clinical trial design and bringing treatments to patients more efficiently, but does not identify accelerating the FDA approval process as a role for AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI can contribute across the entire pipeline, from understanding basic biology to developing and testing new medicines. Early on, it can help researchers make sense of complex data, generate hypotheses, and identify potential drug targets. Then, in discovery, it can help design molecules and prioritize which ones to test.

The key is connecting those predictions to experiments. Biology is incredibly complex, so a promising computational result is really a starting point. If we can create a tighter loop—where AI helps guide experiments, and experimental results improve the models—we can learn faster and make better decisions about what to pursue.

Further downstream, AI can also help with things like identifying patient populations and supporting clinical trial design. Across all of these stages, the opportunity is to give scientists better tools for navigating uncertainty, with the ultimate goal of getting effective treatments to patients.

r001.rationale: The response mentions patient-population identification and clinical-trial design, but does not identify accelerating FDA approval as a potential role for AI.
